tribe: Banu Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza, Quraysh
era: The Hawari — Disciple of the Prophet ﷺ
teaser: 'Every Prophet has a disciple, and my disciple is az-Zubayr.' He was sixteen when he became Muslim.
quran_mention: Aisha applied to him and to Asma the verse «الَّذِينَ اسْتَجَابُوا لِلَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ مِن بَعْدِ مَا أَصَابَهُمُ الْقَرْحُ» — 'those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after injury had befallen them' (3:172).

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: An orphan boy his mother raised hard on purpose
layers.content:
Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy. His kunya was Abu Abdullah. His mother was Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib — which made him the Prophet's ﷺ first cousin.

His father died young, and Safiyya raised him with a hand that shocked the neighbours. Urwa reported that she used to beat him hard, and people told her: you will kill him, you will break his heart, will you destroy the boy? She answered: 'I beat him so that he will be intelligent and will be bold in battle.'

It worked early. As a boy in Makkah he fought a grown man, broke his hand and left him badly beaten. The man was carried past Safiyya, who was pregnant. What happened, she asked. He fought az-Zubayr, they said. She answered them in verse: how did you find Zubayr — soft as cheese or dates, or filled with brass?

He grew into a man neither tall nor short, light-fleshed, dark-hued and hairy, with a thin beard. His hair reached his shoulders; his son Urwa remembered hanging off his back by it as a child. When it turned white, he left it white.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Sixteen years old and fourth or fifth in
layers.content:
Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn Abd ar-Rahman said simply: az-Zubayr became Muslim after Abu Bakr, and was the fourth or fifth Muslim. Hisham ibn Urwa reported from his father that he was sixteen years old.

Think about what that means. Islam at that point was a handful of people in a hostile city, with no protection, no numbers and no argument from success. A sixteen-year-old orphan of Banu Asad joined it before there was any reason to expect it would survive the year. Al-Mubarakpuri lists him among the earliest eight to accept Islam.

What it cost him shows in where he went next: he emigrated to Abyssinia, and the sources say he did so both times. That is a boy leaving Arabia altogether, twice, for the sake of something he had chosen while barely out of childhood.

One report about his later restraint tells you how seriously he took it. His son asked him why he did not narrate from the Prophet ﷺ the way others did — he had never left his side since becoming Muslim. Az-Zubayr answered that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say that whoever tells a lie about him should take a seat in the Fire.
layers.hadith_ref: Az-Zubayr: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, Anyone who tells a lie about me should take a seat in the Fire' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The one who answered before anyone else did
layers.content:
He was twenty-nine at Badr. There were only two horses in the Muslim camp that day and he was on one of them, wearing a yellow head-band. The Prophet ﷺ said afterwards that the angels came down bearing the mark of az-Zubayr.

At Uhud the Quraysh standard-bearer Talhah ibn Abi Talhah, called the Ram of the Battalion, came out on a camel and called for a duel. Az-Zubayr answered it, came down on him, dragged him off the camel and killed him. The Prophet ﷺ said takbir, then said the sentence that became az-Zubayr's name for the rest of history: 'Every Prophet has a disciple, and my disciple is az-Zubayr.' Reports differ over the occasion — Ibn Sa'd places the words at the Ditch, when the Prophet ﷺ asked three times who would bring news of the Banu Qurayzah and az-Zubayr answered all three times.

Aisha told his son Urwa: your parents were among those who answered Allah and the Messenger after they had taken wounds. At the conquest of Makkah he commanded the left flank. Once, sent to Egypt, he was warned of plague there. He said: we come for stabbing and for plague.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 3:172 — «الَّذِينَ اسْتَجَابُوا لِلَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ مِن بَعْدِ مَا أَصَابَهُمُ الْقَرْحُ» — 'those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after injury had befallen them'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ: 'Every Prophet has a disciple and my disciple is az-Zubayr' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: A question about his mother stopped him cold
layers.content:
The hardest day of his life was not a battle against Quraysh. It was the Day of the Camel, when the two halves of the ummah faced each other and az-Zubayr was on the field opposite Ali.

Before the fighting he called his son Abdullah to stand beside him and said: my son, today no one will be killed but a wrongdoer or someone wronged, and I do not think I will be killed except wronged. Then he turned straight to his debts and dictated what to sell.

Ibn Abbas came to him and asked one question: where is Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib, when you fight with your sword against Ali ibn Abi Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib? Az-Zubayr turned back. Jawn ibn Qatada, who was with him, watched him start to shake, weapon and all, and said to himself that this could only be something the man had heard or seen — this, the horseman of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then az-Zubayr sat on his mount and left the field.

Muslims have differed ever since over how to weigh those days, and it is not for a reader eight centuries later to settle it. What the record shows is a man who, given a reason to stop, stopped.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: A debt his son paid by naming its guarantor
layers.content:
He was killed in Wadi as-Siba' on Thursday 10 Jumada al-Akhira 36 AH, riding away from the fighting, aged sixty-four. Umayr ibn Jurmuz rode him down and brought his sword to Ali, who took it and said: by Allah, a sword that often lifted grief from the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — but the times and the deaths are bad. When the killer asked to be admitted, Ali said: give the killer of Safiyya's son the news of the Fire. Then he sat by the grave and wept.

He left almost no cash — some land at al-Ghaba and a few houses — and a debt so large the reports do not agree on the figure. It had a strange cause: when men brought him money to hold, he refused to take it as a deposit and insisted on a loan instead, so that if it were lost the loss would be his. He never took a governorship or a tax office.

His instruction to Abdullah was: if you cannot pay something, ask my Patron for help. Who is your patron, his son asked. 'Allah,' he said. Abdullah said afterwards that whenever a debt defeated him he would say, O Patron of az-Zubayr, settle his debt for me — and it was settled.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: How old was az-Zubayr when he became Muslim?

options.text: Twelve
Sixteen
Twenty-nine
Thirty-five

quiz.citation: Reported from Hisham ibn Urwa — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was twenty-nine at Badr, thirteen years later. Almost half his life as a Muslim was lived before Islam had a city of its own.

quiz.prompt: What title did the Prophet ﷺ give az-Zubayr?

options.text: Al-Amin — the trustworthy of this ummah
Sayf Allah — the sword of Allah
His hawari — his disciple, as every Prophet had one
As-Siddiq — the one who confirms the truth

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Umar was strict about it. When a boy claimed to be the son of the Prophet's ﷺ disciple, he said: only if he is of the family of az-Zubayr — otherwise no. He knew of no one else who held the title.

quiz.prompt: Why did az-Zubayr narrate so few hadith, despite never leaving the Prophet's ﷺ side?

options.text: He could not read or write
He feared the warning against anyone who tells a lie about the Prophet ﷺ
He was away on campaign for most of the Madinan years
He had given his narrations to his son to transmit instead

quiz.citation: Reported from Amr ibn Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had more material than almost anyone and used less of it than almost anyone. Silence, for him, was a form of precision.

quiz.prompt: What did Ibn Abbas say to az-Zubayr on the Day of the Camel?

options.text: He reminded him that the Prophet ﷺ had called him his disciple
He asked where Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib was, while he fought Ali ibn Abi Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib
He told him Aisha had withdrawn from the field
He warned him that his debts would ruin his sons

quiz.citation: Reported from Ikrima from Ibn Abbas — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: One sentence, made entirely of names. He was reminding az-Zubayr that he and Ali shared a grandfather, and that his own mother was that grandfather's daughter. Az-Zubayr turned back.

quiz.prompt: Why did az-Zubayr die owing so much money?

options.text: He had lost his estates in the fitnah
He borrowed to fund expeditions out of his own pocket
He refused to hold money as a deposit and took it as a loan instead, so any loss would be his
He had guaranteed the debts of the whole of Banu Asad

quiz.citation: Reported from Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: A deposit costs the depositor if it is lost; a loan costs the borrower. He chose the version where he carried the risk. His debt was the shape of his scrupulousness.

quiz.prompt: Safiyya was hard on her orphan son on purpose, and he became the Prophet's ﷺ horseman. How do you read the severity you were raised with?

options.text: It made me capable, and I would not undo it
It made me capable and cost me something I am still finding
It was simply harm, whatever came out of it
I was raised gently and sometimes wonder what that cost me

quiz.citation: Reflection on the account of Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note that the sources preserve the neighbours' objection alongside her answer. Even the people recording it did not pretend it was easy to watch.

quiz.prompt: At the Ditch the Prophet ﷺ asked three times who would go, and az-Zubayr answered three times. What usually makes you volunteer?
quiz.slider_label: What moves you to step up

options.text: The silence — I cannot bear a question going unanswered
Knowing I am the one who can actually do it
Wanting the person asking to see me answer
I mostly wait for someone to name me

quiz.citation: Reported from Jabir ibn Abdullah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He answered the second and third time knowing the first answer had already been heard. That repetition is what the Prophet ﷺ took his hand for.

quiz.prompt: Az-Zubayr knew more hadith than most and narrated less than most, out of fear of getting a word wrong. Where do you sit on speaking about the sacred?

options.text: I speak freely — silence lets error spread
I speak only about what I have actually checked
I stay quiet because I am afraid of being wrong
I stay quiet because I have never really been asked

quiz.citation: Reflection on az-Zubayr's restraint in narration — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His son found the silence strange enough to ask about it. Restraint that no one can explain from outside is usually restraint with a reason inside.

quiz.prompt: One question about his family made az-Zubayr leave a battlefield he had chosen to be on. What could stop you mid-course?

options.text: A person I respect saying it plainly
Realising who I am hurting on the other side
Almost nothing, once I have publicly committed
Only my own conscience, in private, later

quiz.citation: Reflection on the account of Ibn Abbas and az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Turning back cost him more than staying would have; he was killed on the road out. Withdrawing is not always the safe option.

quiz.prompt: 'If you cannot pay something, ask my Patron' — and the Patron was Allah. What do you actually hand over when you say you are relying on Allah?

options.text: The outcome — I still do all the work
The part I genuinely cannot reach
I say it more than I mean it
I hand over too early, and call waiting reliance

quiz.citation: Reported from Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abdullah spent years selling land, calling at the pilgrimage and negotiating with creditors. The reliance and the labour were the same act, not alternatives.
